prompt: Which component of the control plane is the only one that reads and writes etcd?
hint: Every other component reaches the data through it.

choices.text: The scheduler
choices.why: The scheduler writes a pod's node through the API server, like everyone else.

choices.text: The controller manager
choices.why: Its controllers create objects through the API server; they never open etcd.

choices.text: The API server
choices.why: Right. Its `--etcd-servers` flag points at etcd, and every check it makes depends on there being no other door.

choices.text: The kubelet on the control-plane node
choices.why: That kubelet runs etcd as a static pod; it does not read its data.

prompt: The control plane's components are pods, yet pods are created through the API server. How does the API server start on a fresh node?

choices.text: kubeadm starts it directly and keeps it running
choices.why: kubeadm writes the files and exits; it does not supervise anything.

choices.text: The kubelet runs it from a file on disk
choices.why: Right. The kubelet watches that directory and needs no API server to run what is in it.

choices.text: etcd starts it when the database comes up
choices.why: etcd stores data and starts nothing; it is a static pod too.

choices.text: The scheduler places it on the control-plane node
choices.why: The scheduler works through the API server, so it cannot be what starts it.

prompt: Every object is stored in etcd under a key that begins with `/___/`, followed by its type, namespace and name.
Why is the kubelet a systemd service on the node rather than a pod?
hint: Ask what would have to start it.

choices.text: Pods cannot run on worker nodes
choices.why: Ana's pods ran on both workers.

choices.text: It needs more memory than any pod is allowed to have
choices.why: Memory has nothing to do with it; the question is what starts it.

choices.text: kube-proxy refuses to route to it otherwise
choices.why: kube-proxy routes Service traffic to pods, not to the kubelet.

choices.text: It is what runs pods, so nothing could run it
choices.why: Right. The kubelet asks the runtime to start pods; something below it, systemd here, has to start the kubelet.

prompt: Match each node component with the question it answers.
hint: Four things run on every node.

pairs.right: Which pods should run here, and are they running?
How is a container actually started?
Which pod does a Service address lead to?
What address and routes does a new pod get?

right_distractors: Which node should an unscheduled pod go to?

prompt: A colleague reads the name kube-proxy and concludes every request to a Service passes through that process. What would show them otherwise?
hint: Where does kube-proxy put its work?

choices.text: `crictl ps`, which shows kube-proxy as a container
choices.why: Being a container says nothing about whether traffic flows through it.

choices.text: The node's kernel rules, which rewrite the packets themselves
choices.why: Right. kube-proxy writes iptables or nftables rules and steps aside; lesson 17 reads them.

choices.text: `systemctl is-active`, which shows it is not a service
choices.why: Whether systemd runs it is unrelated to the path a packet takes.

choices.text: The CNI directory, which holds its routes
choices.why: That directory configures the network plugin, not kube-proxy.

prompt: Put in order the components that acted on Ana's new deployment, as the events recorded them.
hint: The events were sorted by when they were written.
items: The deployment controller makes a ReplicaSet
The ReplicaSet controller makes a pod with no node
The scheduler writes a node into the pod
The kubelet on that node starts the container
trap: Each step needs the object the previous one wrote: no pod before its ReplicaSet, no container before a node is chosen.

prompt: With the scheduler stopped, Ana scaled the shop from one copy to three. What did `kubectl get pods` show?
hint: Which steps of the chain still had someone to do them?

choices.text: Only the original pod, since scaling was refused
choices.why: `deployment.apps/shop scaled` was printed; the API server accepted the change.

choices.text: The original pod running and two new ones `Pending`
choices.why: Right. The controllers made the pods; nobody chose a node for them.

choices.text: Three pods `Running`, all on the control-plane node
choices.why: Without a scheduler no pod gets a node, on the control plane or anywhere.

choices.text: No pods at all: the running one stopped too
choices.why: The running pod kept running; a scheduler is only needed to place new ones.

prompt: The API server of a cluster goes down for ten minutes. During that time, what happens to the shop's pods that were already running?
hint: Who keeps a running pod running?

choices.text: They stop, because the kubelet loses its instructions
choices.why: The kubelet keeps the pods it already has; it only cannot learn of new ones.

choices.text: They are moved to the nodes that can still reach etcd
choices.why: Nodes never reach etcd, and nothing can move a pod while the API server is down.

choices.text: They keep serving, and nothing about them can change
choices.why: Right. A control plane that stops is a cluster that cannot change, not one that stops serving.

choices.text: They restart in a loop until the API server returns
choices.why: Nothing restarts them; their containers keep the processes they have.

prompt: Which of these run as pods on the laptop's cluster? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of them cannot, and one is a database inside a pod.

choices.text: kube-apiserver
choices.why: Right: a static pod on the control-plane node.

choices.text: etcd
choices.why: Right: also a static pod.

choices.text: kubelet
choices.why: It is a systemd service; it is what runs pods.

choices.text: kube-proxy
choices.why: Right: one per node, from a DaemonSet.

choices.text: containerd
choices.why: The runtime is a service the kubelet talks to.
